en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Acelaka-vagga 49.
The Training Rule on Living with an Army.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, on having some business, the group-of-six monks went to the army and stayed with the army for more than three nights.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying:
"How can these ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, stay with an army?"
“It is our misfortune, it is our ill-luck, that we live for the sake of our livelihood and for the sake of our wives and children, and dwell with an army.
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and lamenting.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... they grumbled, complained, and lamented:
“How indeed can the group of six monks stay with an army for more than three nights?
… [The Buddha asked: “Is it true, monks, that you stay with an army for more than three nights?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, stay with an army for more than three nights?
This, foolish men, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:

“If there should be some reason for that monk to go to an army, he may stay with the army for two or three nights. If he should stay longer than that, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya). “If there should be some reason for that monk to go to an army”:
[this means] if there should be some reason whatsoever for that monk to go to an army.
There may be a reason; there may be a duty.
"That bhikkhu may stay with the army for two or three nights" means he may stay for two or three nights.
If he should stay longer than that:
on the fourth day, when the sun has set, if he stays with the army, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If he stays with the army for more than three nights while perceiving it to be more than three nights, there is an offense of expiation.
If he stays with an army for more than three nights while being in doubt, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If he stays with an army for more than three nights while perceiving it as less, there is an offense of expiation.
If he stays for less than three nights while perceiving it as more, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is less than two nights and he is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is less than two nights and he perceives it as less, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
He dwells for two or three nights;
he dwells for less than two or three nights;
having dwelt for two nights, he departs before dawn on the third night and dwells again.
He dwells as one who is ill;
he dwells on account of a task for one who is ill;
or the army is besieged by a hostile force.
He is hindered by something; he is in times of distress;
he is insane.
"For one who is a first offender":
the ninth training rule concerning staying with an army is finished.
